source.version_note: Supplied publisher PDF, Internet Research 36(3), 1073–1092. Crossref records online publication on 13 January 2026 and print publication on 19 May 2026; PDF file creation in May is not the first-publication date.
source.verification_method: All 20 supplied text pages read, including notes, references and appendices. Figures 1–4, Tables 1–5 and Tables A1–A2 visually checked on pages 5, 7–10, 12–13 and 16. Crossref verifies article identity/dates and three cited records. External OSF materials, raw data and analysis code were not inspected or reproduced.

citation.title: Under pressure: how widespread vs severe competitor unethical practices shape responsible artificial intelligence deployment

reading.source_scope_note: Three online vignette studies (249 and 304 U.S. MTurk participations; 159 retained U.K. Prolific participants). Studies 1–2 measure hypothetical launch recommendations; Study 3 evaluates an already-made recommendation and conditional accountability items. No actual product launch, model behavior or consumer harm was observed. Reporting and mediation-design conflicts remain unresolved.
access_limits: External OSF full stimuli, scale anchors, preregistrations if any, raw data and code were not independently read or executed. Unresolved coding/sign conflicts require those outputs or author clarification.
The paper cites classic regulatory-focus and moral-disengagement sources, but those original books/articles were not fully read here. Metadata checks are not independent paper credit.

The two MTurk samples sum to 553 participations, but their cross-study uniqueness is not explicitly established. The combined three-study total is 712 participations, not demonstrated 712 independently unique people.

study.design: Three randomized competitive-context vignette studies. Study 1 uses measured regulatory-focus scores; Study 2 crosses competitive context with bundled employee-and-company goal descriptions; Study 3 has randomized between-person context plus fixed-order within-person conditional accountability item sets.

samples.focus_measure: Four promotion and four prevention items; alpha .84/.85. Promotion minus prevention, then mean-centering, gives the moderator.

samples.target: Approximately 50 per cell in a 2×3 design
samples.focus_manipulation: Alex and MarkTech both described as promotion-focused or both prevention-focused; these are not independently crossed.

study.competition_contexts: Control supplies no competitor comparison. Horizontal describes 95% of firms in Studies 1–2 and 90% in Study 3 using similar targeted-marketing/personalized-pricing AI. Vertical describes a main competitor using the same system plus microphone data collection; the Study 1 appendix additionally specifies sale of sensitive data without explicit consent. Competitor number, prevalence and severity are bundled rather than orthogonally manipulated.
study.outcomes: Studies 1–2 reverse-code 1–7 launch agreement so higher values mean more cautious/nonlaunch choices. Study 3 first asks ethicality/justice/moral acceptability of a recommendation already made, then asks all nine accountability items in fixed Control–Horizontal–Vertical order. Its outcome scale direction conflicts across labels and prose and is not resolved from the PDF.
study.study1_results: At centered focus 0, horizontal versus control b=−.70, p=.023; vertical b=.42, p=.165. Vertical×focus b=−.30, p=.070; horizontal×focus b=.04, p=.772. Table 2 probes actual values −1.90, .35 and 2.10; the low-focus vertical contrast is +1.00, p=.024, but this does not make the direct interaction p<.05.
study.study2_results: ANOVA focus×context F(2,298)=4.05, p=.018. With promotion=0 and prevention=1, vertical×prevention b=+1.20, p=.012; horizontal×prevention b=.06, p=.894. Prevention vertical versus control b=.85, p=.011; promotion vertical b≈−.35, p=.305. Horizontal contrasts: promotion −.61, p=.057; prevention −.54, p=.121. Table 3 contains coefficient/t/CI sign inconsistencies.
study.study3_results: Between-context ethical-evaluation ANOVA F(2,156)=4.68, p=.011, eta-squared .06. Horizontal–control difference is reported +.86, Tukey p=.007, but prose calls this less ethical while Figure 4 labels higher scores ethicality. Within-person conditional accountability differences are H−C=−.83, t(158)=−9.55, and V−C=−.96, t(158)=−10.24, both p<.001. These paired comparisons are not the randomized between-context effects.
study.mediation: PROCESS Model 4 uses the accountability item set matched to assigned context, changing mediator wording with treatment. Reported aH=−1.01, aV=−.80 and b=−.32 yield positive indirect effects .32/.25 with bootstrap CIs excluding zero. The outcome precedes the mediator, the mediator is not a common invariant instrument, and Table 5 conflicts internally; distinct causal mechanisms are not established.

summary: Add promotion focus and prevention focus as distinct goal orientations. Enrich existing moral disengagement, diffusion of responsibility, advantageous comparison and unethical pro-organizational behavior with qualified human-vignette evidence. Do not add new rows for horizontal/vertical competition labels or infer universal launch effects, actual AI motives or experimentally established causal mediation.

findings.definition: Orienting goal pursuit toward advancement, gains and aspirations, with attention to achieving desired outcomes.
findings.origin: Regulatory-focus theory / human motivation and organizational decision-making
findings.ai_evidence_status: Measured human orientation in Study 1 and a bundled employee/company description in Study 2; no AI regulatory-focus mechanism was tested.
findings.ai_proposal: Compare an assistant’s recommendations under gain/aspiration versus duty/security goal instructions while holding task facts, authorization, rights and outcome probabilities constant. Score changes in evidence use, authorized exploration and safeguards rather than assume a human motivation from wording.
findings.novelty_rationale: A gain-and-aspiration goal orientation is distinct from egoism, positive affect, risk preference, loss weighting and a simultaneous approach–avoidance conflict. No existing name/alias or definition covers this orientation.

evidence.quote: hopes, wishes, and aspirations within the organization.

findings.evidence_scope: Regulatory-focus theory distinguishes aspirational growth goals from duties/security. In Study 2, promotion descriptions are crossed with competitor contexts, but individual and organization descriptions are bundled; ethical effects depend on context and several printed statistics conflict.
findings.boundary: Promotion focus is not a diagnosis, inherent wrongdoing, a guarantee of innovation or a fixed risk appetite. People can also have prevention concerns. An AI instruction emphasizing gains is an operational manipulation, not proof of intrinsic desire or personal aspirations.

findings.definition: Orienting goal pursuit toward security, duties and obligations, with attention to avoiding losses and undesired outcomes.
findings.origin: Regulatory-focus theory / human motivation and organizational decision-making
findings.ai_evidence_status: Measured human orientation in Study 1 and a bundled employee/company description in Study 2; no AI regulatory-focus mechanism was tested.
findings.ai_proposal: Vary duty/security versus gain/aspiration instructions with identical evidence, permissions and stakes. Evaluate proportionate checks and compliance while detecting unnecessary refusal, unjustified deference or acceptance of harmful industry practices. Test outcomes separately from motive labels.
findings.novelty_rationale: Duty/security-oriented goal pursuit differs from loss aversion’s asymmetric value weighting, status-quo bias’s unwarranted inertia and experiential avoidance of internal distress. It does not require a simultaneous attraction/aversion conflict.

evidence.quote: prioritizes stability and security, aiming to minimize losses and maintain the status quo.
duties, responsibilities, and obligations within the

findings.evidence_scope: Theory and Study 2 framing emphasize obligations and prevention of failures. Under the severe-competitor scenario, prevention has a more cautious launch contrast than promotion, with direct interaction p=.012 in Study 2 but p=.070 in Study 1. This is conditional vignette evidence, not a universal ethical advantage.
findings.boundary: Prevention focus need not mean risk aversion, inflexible obedience or ethical conduct. Protecting an organization’s losses can conflict with others’ rights. Separate its duty/security reference from loss weighting and from whether caution is warranted. No human anxiety or duty feeling in an AI is established.

findings.definition: Diluting felt personal responsibility for harmful conduct by treating responsibility as shared among multiple actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing concept covers this meaning; retain its stable ID and add the present source with explicit design and inference limits.

evidence.quote: widespread adoption activates diffusion of responsibility.
Each participant responded to three items per condition (Control, Horizontal,
mediator matched to the moral accountability associated with the treatment condition,

findings.evidence_scope: The paper explicitly theorizes widespread competitor adoption as a diffusion cue. Study 3 respondents endorse less accountability for a counterfactual many-competitor item set than a no-competitor set. Fixed order, wording and matched-by-treatment mediator selection prevent a clean or unique causal-mechanism conclusion.
findings.boundary: Shared legitimate duties and industry prevalence do not erase individual obligations. Conditional endorsement differences are not actual misconduct or proof of felt AI responsibility; retain the distinction between within-person item contrasts and randomized context effects.

findings.definition: Making harmful conduct seem acceptable or less blameworthy by contrasting it with conduct portrayed as worse.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing concept covers this meaning; retain its stable ID and add the present source with explicit design and inference limits.

findings.evidence_scope: The severe-competitor condition is designed as advantageous comparison, but prevention-focused participants can instead become more cautious in Study 2. Study 3 lower conditional-accountability ratings do not establish that this unique process caused an actual launch or that comparison always excuses misconduct.
findings.boundary: A worse comparator may highlight unacceptable risks and prompt caution. The ethical status of the focal action still requires relevant rights and harms. The study does not demonstrate an inevitable comparison-induced decline or a distinct causal mediator.

findings.definition: Suspending or bypassing moral self-regulation so harmful conduct can be justified before or after it occurs.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing concept covers this meaning; retain its stable ID and add the present source with explicit design and inference limits.

evidence.quote: Participants then completed nine accountability items
with the mediator matched to the moral accountability associated with the treatment condition,

findings.evidence_scope: Provides an explicit theoretical application and original human ratings in AI deployment vignettes. Study 3 labels condition-specific accountability items as disengagement and reports indirect effects, but outcome-first order, different mediator wording by treatment and table conflicts prevent causal validation of the two proposed pathways.
findings.boundary: A significant bootstrap indirect estimate is not proof of a unique moral-disengagement process. Accountability, evaluation of ethics and actual conduct differ. Reduced conditional responsibility can reflect framing or question order; no model conscience or hidden mental state is measured.

findings.definition: Actions intended to benefit an organization or its members that violate ethical standards or others’ legitimate interests.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing concept covers this meaning; retain its stable ID and add the present source with explicit design and inference limits.

evidence.quote: to increase profits and build technological
Alex had recommended implementing the AI.

findings.evidence_scope: The paper calls the focal launch recommendation AI-based UPB and uses profit-oriented marketing/privacy vignettes. Studies 1–2 measure stated recommendations, not enacted launch decisions; Study 3 measures judgments of a recommendation already made. Ethicality coding conflicts are retained rather than converted into a uniform effect.
findings.boundary: An organizational benefit does not itself prove unethical intent or violation. Consent, data provenance, discrimination and rights determine the relevant boundary. No real customer harm, actual organizational misconduct or behavior by an AI system is established.

findings.definition: Repeated departures from standards become accepted organisational practice.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing concept covers this meaning; retain its stable ID and add the present source with explicit design and inference limits.

evidence.quote: race to the bottom that normalizes irresponsible AI deployment.

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion proposes a race to the bottom as potentially unethical AI practices become widespread. No longitudinal industry data, repeated escalation manipulation or changing market threshold is observed; this is a conceptual boundary note.
findings.boundary: A single prevalence vignette cannot establish gradual normalization, actual industry adoption or an inevitable slippery slope. The paper’s proposed market transition remains an explanatory possibility.

source_corrections.issue: Page 3 says promotion-focused behavior increases AI-based UPB; page 4 says promotion-focused goals lower UPB, citing the same paper.
source_corrections.resolution: Record the internal contradiction. Crossref confirms DOI 10.1016/j.chbah.2024.100112, authors, title and 2025 volume 3 article 100112, but its complete text was not reviewed here; do not choose a direction from metadata.

source_corrections.issue: Probes are called both mean/±1 SD and 16th/50th/84th percentiles. Table 2 uses −1.90, .35 and 2.10 despite mean-centering. Repeated adjacent paragraphs say H2b is supported and contrary to prediction.
source_corrections.resolution: Use actual probe values; .35 is not centered mean zero and the values are not symmetric ±SD. Table 1 mean-zero vertical .42 and Table 2 .35-focus vertical .32 are compatible, not contradictory. Preserve direct interaction p=.070 and the counter-prediction pattern rather than treating selected-probe significance as conclusive moderation.

source_corrections.issue: Plots are labeled AI-based UPB although the methods/results reverse-code the outcome so higher scores mean more ethical/nonlaunch choices.
source_corrections.resolution: Preserve the explicitly stated reverse coding for Studies 1–2; do not read taller bars as more unethical launches from the caption alone.

source_corrections.issue: Prevention Focus b=−.64 and t=−1.92 conflict with CI[−.02,1.30], centered at +.64. Vertical×Prevention b=+1.20 and CI[.27,2.13] conflict with negative t=−2.53. Figure 3 also depicts the prevention control mean above the promotion control mean.
source_corrections.resolution: These are visible published table discrepancies, not extraction artifacts. They suggest sign/transcription problems but do not authorize silently replacing the original coefficient/output. Require raw regression output to repair.

source_corrections.issue: Prose attributes horizontal b=−.61, p=.057 to prevention, but promotion=0 and Table 4 assign it to promotion; prevention is −.54, p=.121.
source_corrections.resolution: Retain the coding/Table 4 distinction and do not call .057 or demographic-adjusted .051 p<.05. Note 4 reports −.58, p=.014 after dropping the nonsignificant interaction: that is a different, constrained regression, not either original simple effect.

source_corrections.location: Pages 11–12 and Figure 4, Study 3 ethicality direction
source_corrections.issue: Horizontal difference +.86 and a higher ethicality-labeled bar accompany prose calling the decision less ethical. The supplied text does not give endpoints sufficient to settle outcome orientation.
source_corrections.resolution: Report a changed evaluation with unresolved direction, rather than assert increased ethicality or increased unethicality. No invented reverse coding or corrected raw means.

source_corrections.issue: H3 states accountability is mediated by disengagement; the fitted model instead uses perceived accountability as mediator of treatment to ethicality. The same responsibility items are labeled moral disengagement. All participants answer every conditional item set in fixed order, while the fitted mediator selects different wording by treatment.
source_corrections.resolution: Distinguish the stated hypothesis, statistical model, item-set contrasts and randomized effects. Reduced conditional accountability is not unique measurement of each distinct mechanism. The outcome was answered first; positive indirect estimates do not identify a causal psychological pathway.

source_corrections.issue: Vertical direct effect −.20 conflicts with positive t=.72 and CI[−.35,.75], centered +.20; −.20+.25 is not the printed total +.45. Horizontal total b=.45 conflicts with SE=.28,t=3.06,CI[.30,1.41], and direct .54 plus indirect .32; the earlier Tukey difference is .86. Horizontal indirect CI is visibly malformed as [0.100.0.59].
source_corrections.resolution: Record the incompatible fields. The likely positive vertical direct effect and approximately .86 horizontal total are consistency diagnostics, not substituted results. Prose supplies horizontal indirect CI[.10,.59]. Require code/output before a definitive repair. Tukey-adjusted and regression p values need not match.

source_corrections.issue: Printed JAIS page range 281–252 is reversed and incorrect.
source_corrections.resolution: Crossref DOI 10.17705/1jais.00662 verifies volume 22(2), pages 281–303. This is a metadata correction, not a full reading of the editorial.

source_corrections.issue: Managing Artificial Intelligence is printed as pages 433–1450.
source_corrections.resolution: Crossref DOI 10.25300/MISQ/2021/16274 verifies MIS Quarterly 45(3), pages 1433–1450. No full reading of that cited paper is claimed.

methodological_limits: Hypothetical low-stakes online responses are not observed organizational launch behavior or measured deployed-AI misconduct. The authors explicitly acknowledge external-validity limits and call for professional replication.

A targeted-marketing/personalized-pricing system and use of third-party data are not intrinsically unethical in every context. Consent, data provenance, discrimination, lawful purpose and affected rights matter. Note 2 articulates the authors’ privacy rationale; the vignette is not a complete legal or fairness audit.

Competition conditions bundle number/prevalence with an additional, explicitly severe violation. They do not independently estimate the causal effects of competitor count and severity or a naturally evolving market threshold.

Measured Study 1 focus cannot be causally attributed; subtracting two scales obscures their separate levels and does not demonstrate that the orientations are a single bipolar trait. Study 2 varies employee and organization descriptions together and cannot isolate their contributions.

At p<.05, the Study 1 vertical interaction is not significant; a significant low-focus simple effect and nonsignificant high-focus effect are not themselves a significant difference. Null horizontal interactions do not establish exact invariance or equivalence.
Study 3 changes the outcome from personal launch recommendation to moral evaluation of someone else’s recommendation. It is not a direct behavioral replication of Studies 1–2.

Study 3 within-person conditional-item contrasts confound wording/context and fixed order. The paired results use every respondent, not separate randomized groups. The matched-by-treatment mediator changes its measurement instrument with treatment; reliability alpha does not establish measurement invariance.

Statistical mediation with a post-outcome, nonrandomized mediator does not identify a causal mechanism. Separate diffusion and advantageous-comparison pathways were not independently experimentally identified.
Source-table signs, outcome labels, probe labels and hypothesis descriptions conflict. Exact statistical repairs require the external analysis materials, which were not inspected.

The predicted transition from vertical to horizontal industry misconduct and suggested audits, alliances and approval gates are theoretical/managerial proposals, not longitudinal market observations or tested interventions.

cross_paper_learning.finding: As in the marketing-manager experiments, a prewritten recommendation or vignette response must remain separate from actual deployment. Study-specific coding and outcome manipulations matter; do not collapse every profit-oriented scenario into one universal ethical effect.

Advantageous comparison already has an entry from the moral-cover synthesis. This paper adds original human-vignette data but its mechanism labels and statistical mediation are not uniquely identified process evidence.

Responsibility distribution is not automatically diffusion. Here the authors specifically measure lower conditional accountability, but item wording/order and matched mediator selection still prevent treating it as a clean test of the mechanism.
Preserve inconsistent printed statistics and construct labels instead of resolving them by trusting a summary paragraph or inferring missing raw values.

deferred.term: Horizontal unethical competition / vertical unethical competition
deferred.reason: Useful contextual manipulation labels, not two new independently demonstrated psychological behaviors. Their intended mechanisms enrich existing diffusion and advantageous-comparison entries.

Use regulatory-focus theory as the shared theoretical family for promotion/prevention entries. Fit is discussed through secondary citations but is not independently crossed from employee/company orientation or directly measured here; do not add a separate validated fit effect from this paper.

Secondary explanatory account citing Welsh et al. 2015; no gradual-versus-abrupt trajectory is manipulated in these studies. Do not count that cited paper as read or add a new directly demonstrated trajectory mechanism.

deferred.term: Conformity / social proof / normalization of deviance
deferred.reason: Conceptually adjacent to high competitor prevalence, but no independent measure establishes each additional mechanism. The existing normalization entry receives a boundary-only note; no synonymous new rows.

limitations: Canonical article identity and two bibliography page ranges were externally verified. The conflicting 2025-paper summary and the study’s internal statistical/coding conflicts remain unresolved; no author was contacted.
No claim that promotion focus is inherently unethical, prevention focus guarantees safety, or a model possesses either human motive. No automatic normative or harm edges are added.
